title: Chat Messenger
prompt: Design a mobile messenger with one-to-one and group chats. Messages should arrive instantly when people are online, wait for them when they are not, and show sent, delivered and read ticks.

clarify.q: How big can a group get?
clarify.why: Up to a few hundred members, we can write a copy of each message pointer per member. Tens of thousands (broadcast channels) needs a pull model, like a feed.

clarify.q: Does the server keep message history, or only hold messages until delivered?
clarify.why: Store-until-delivered keeps storage tiny. Keeping history (for new devices and search) makes us a database of every message ever sent, with retention costs.

clarify.q: Can one user be logged in on several devices at once?
clarify.why: Multi-device turns 'deliver to a user' into 'deliver to each device and keep each one's sync position', and read state must sync across devices.
With E2E the server only routes ciphertext. Server-side search, previews in push notifications and history for new devices all become harder.

clarify.q: Do we need read receipts and typing indicators in groups?
clarify.why: Per-message per-member receipts in a 500-person group are 500 updates per message. The answer decides whether we store watermarks instead.

clarify.q: Do we show online status and last seen to everyone, or just contacts?
clarify.why: Presence is the noisiest traffic in a chat system. Limiting who can see it limits how many people we must notify on every change.
Media goes to object storage through upload URLs; the chat message only carries a reference. That keeps the real-time path small.

functional: Send and receive text messages in 1:1 and group chats (up to 500 members).
Messages in one conversation appear in the same order for every participant and device.
Offline users receive missed messages on reconnect, plus a push notification.
Sent, delivered and read status per message; online and last-seen presence.
A user's several devices stay in sync, including what has been read.
nonFunctional: Online-to-online delivery p99 under 300 ms within a region.
No acknowledged message is ever lost (durable before the sender sees one tick).
No duplicates shown when clients retry on flaky mobile networks.
99.99% availability for sending; presence may be briefly stale.
Handle 200 M concurrent connections at peak.
outOfScope: End-to-end encryption key exchange (we note where it changes the design).

assumptions: 500 M daily active users, 40 messages sent per user per day
Average message delivered to 1.5 other users, each with 2 devices
Stored message about 300 B with metadata; history kept 30 days on the server
40% of DAU online at peak; one gateway server holds 100 k connections
Clients send a heartbeat every 30 s

steps.label: Device deliveries
steps.result: ≈ 700 k pushes over sockets per second

steps.label: Storage
steps.math: 20 B × 300 B = 6 TB/day; × 30 days = 180 TB; × 3 replicas = 540 TB
steps.result: ≈ 0.5 PB on disk: a wide-column store across many nodes

steps.label: Gateway fleet
steps.math: 500 M × 40% = 200 M connections; 200 M / 100 k = 2 000 servers
steps.result: ≈ 2 000 gateway servers, plus headroom for deploys

steps.label: Heartbeats
steps.result: Far too many to write to a database: keep liveness in gateway memory

estimates.takeaway: Three numbers drive the design. 230 k messages/s needs a sharded store with a cheap per-conversation write. 200 M open sockets means a large stateful gateway tier kept separate from stateless logic. 6.7 M heartbeats/s means presence must only publish changes, never every heartbeat.

api.note: One long-lived socket per device. Server replies with missed messages since lastInboxSeq, then live traffic.
clientMsgId is a UUID generated on the phone; retries reuse it so the server dedupes.
Client ack advances the device's sync cursor.
HTTP for scrolling back through history; keeps the socket for live traffic.
Client uploads to object storage directly, then sends a message with mediaRef.

entities.name: Conversation
entities.why: Holds the counter that orders messages. Strongly consistent row update, low contention per row.

entities.name: Message
entities.store: Cassandra, partition (conversationId, month), cluster by seq desc
entities.why: Append-only, read by conversation in seq order. Time bucket stops big groups making unbounded partitions.

entities.name: Inbox
entities.store: Cassandra, partition userId, cluster by inboxSeq
entities.why: One tiny pointer per member per message. Gives each device a single cursor to sync from.

entities.name: MemberState
entities.why: Receipts as two numbers per member instead of one row per message per member.

entities.name: Session
entities.store: Redis, key sess:{userId}, TTL refreshed by gateway
entities.why: Routing table: where to send a live message. Rebuildable from gateways if lost.

data.note: Ordering comes from Conversation.nextSeq; storage of the body goes to Cassandra keyed by conversation. The inbox is a per-user index that makes reconnect sync one range read. Sessions are soft state with TTLs, so a crashed gateway's entries expire by themselves.

hld.summary:
Phones keep one WebSocket to a gateway. Gateways are thin and stateful: they hold sockets, track heartbeats, and forward frames to the chat service, which is stateless. The chat service dedupes by clientMsgId, takes the next sequence number for the conversation, writes the message and one inbox pointer per member, and acks the sender (one tick).

For delivery it looks up each recipient's devices in the session registry and publishes to the owning gateway's channel on a pub/sub bus. Recipients with no live device get a push notification and will sync from their inbox cursor on reconnect. Receipts and presence travel the same bus as small events.

diagram.title: Messenger components
diagram.src:
flowchart LR

  B[Recipient phone] --> LB
  LB --> G[WebSocket gateways]
  G --> CS[Chat service]
  CS --> CV[("Conversations and seq, MySQL")]
  CS --> MS[("Messages and inboxes, Cassandra")]
  CS --> SR[("Session registry, Redis")]

  G --> PR[Presence service]

flows.title: Alice sends to Bob, both online
steps: Alice's phone sends a frame with a new clientMsgId; it shows the message with a clock icon.
Chat service checks clientMsgId, increments nextSeq for the conversation, writes the message and Bob's and Alice's inbox pointers.
Chat service acks Alice with seq: one tick.
It finds Bob's two devices in the session registry and publishes to their gateways' channels.
Bob's phone acks; a deliveredUpTo receipt flows back to Alice's devices: two ticks.

flows.title: Bob was offline and reconnects
steps: No live session was found, so a push notification was sent with a short preview (or 'New message' under E2E).
Bob opens the app; the socket connects with lastInboxSeq 9 120.
Gateway asks the chat service for inbox entries after 9 120, fetches the messages in batches, streams them.
Bob's device acks the highest inboxSeq it stored; receipts go out as one watermark per conversation.

flows.title: Bob reads on his laptop
steps: Laptop sends readUpTo seq 512 for the conversation.
Chat service updates MemberState for Bob and publishes the event.
Bob's phone clears the unread badge; Alice's devices show blue ticks up to 512.

deepDives.title: Message ordering within a conversation
deepDives.problem: Two people in a group send at the same instant through different gateways and different chat-service instances. Every device must show the same order, and a device must be able to tell whether it has missed something. Phone clocks are wrong, server clocks drift by milliseconds, and retries on bad networks can send the same message twice.

options.name: Client timestamps
options.how: Each phone stamps its message and everyone sorts by that time.
cons: Phone clocks can be minutes off
Two devices may sort differently on ties
A malicious client can reorder history

options.name: Server receive timestamp
options.how: Chat service stamps the time on arrival and readers sort by it.
cons: Different servers have slightly different clocks
Cannot detect gaps: no way to know a message is missing

options.name: Per-conversation sequence counter
options.how: Atomic increment of Conversation.nextSeq on the conversation's shard in the same flow as the write; clients order by seq.
pros: One total order per conversation, same on every device
Gaps are detectable, which makes sync simple
Contention is per conversation, which is tiny
cons: An extra consistent write per message
A failed write after taking a seq leaves a harmless gap

options.name: Single-writer partition
options.how: Route each conversation to one Kafka partition; the consumer that owns it assigns seq in memory.
pros: Very high throughput, no DB counter
cons: Failover must fence the old owner or seqs collide
Adds queue latency to every message

deepDives.choice: Per-conversation counter. 230 k/s spread over billions of conversations means almost no row ever sees more than a few increments per second, and 50 MySQL shards each take about 4.6 k increments/s on average (231 k / 50) and about 9 k at peak, which is comfortable. Clients sync with 'seq greater than my last', so gaps from failed writes do not matter. The sender's phone dedupes and orders its own pending messages locally by clientMsgId, then snaps them into seq order on ack. Order across conversations is not promised and not needed. If one conversation became extremely hot (a 100 k member channel), I would move it to the single-writer model.

deepDives.title: Delivery guarantees and read receipts
deepDives.problem: Mobile networks drop mid-send. The sender must know the server has the message, the recipient's device must not lose or duplicate it, and receipts in a 500-member group must not create 500 writes per message.

options.name: Per-message receipt rows
options.how: Store a row per (message, member) with delivered and read times.
cons: A 500 member group sending 100 messages writes 50 000 receipt rows
Receipt traffic exceeds message traffic

options.name: Per-member watermarks
options.how: Each member has deliveredUpTo and readUpTo seq per conversation. A message is read by a member if its seq is at or below their readUpTo.
pros: One small update covers many messages
Matches how people read: in order, up to a point
cons: Cannot represent reading message 10 but not message 9 (fine for chat)
'Read by' list needs a scan of members

deepDives.choice: Watermarks, and an ack at every hop. The sender keeps the message in a local outbox and retries with the same clientMsgId until it gets the seq ack: that gives at-least-once to the server, and dedupe makes it effectively once. The recipient acks by inboxSeq; until it does, the message stays in its inbox and is re-sent on reconnect. Receipt events are coalesced on the client (send one readUpTo after the user stops scrolling for a second). In groups larger than about 50, show 'read by N' on demand instead of pushing every receipt to every member.

diagram.title: Send, store, deliver, receipt
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Alice phone
  participant GA as Gateway A
  participant C as Chat service
  participant DB as Message store
  participant GB as Gateway B
  participant B as Bob phone
  A->>GA: send clientMsgId and body
  GA->>C: forward
  C->>DB: take seq, write message and inbox pointers
  C-->>A: ack with seq, one tick
  C->>GB: publish to Bob's gateway channel
  GB->>B: message with seq and inboxSeq
  B-->>GB: ack inboxSeq
  GB->>C: deliveredUpTo seq
  C-->>A: receipt event, two ticks

deepDives.title: The WebSocket gateway and presence
deepDives.problem: 200 M sockets on 2 000 servers. Any chat-service instance must find the right gateway for a recipient fast, gateways restart during deploys, and presence (online, last seen, typing) changes constantly. Sending every heartbeat or every flap to every contact would dwarf message traffic.

options.name: Sticky routing by userId hash
options.how: Consistent hashing sends each user to a fixed gateway, so routing is a computation, not a lookup.
cons: Multi-device users may land on different hosts anyway
Rebalancing on scale-out moves many sockets at once

options.name: Session registry plus per-gateway channels
options.how: Gateways write userId to deviceId to gatewayId into Redis with a TTL; each gateway subscribes to its own pub/sub channel.
pros: Gateways can drain and reconnect clients freely
cons: One extra lookup per delivery (cacheable)
Registry must survive or be rebuilt

deepDives.choice: Registry plus per-gateway channels. Presence lives in gateway memory: a missed heartbeat for 60 s or a socket close marks the device away. Only transitions are published, after a 10–20 s grace period so a phone switching from Wi-Fi to 4G does not flap. Presence is subscribed lazily: you receive status updates only for the conversations you have open on screen, not for all 300 contacts. Last seen is written to storage at most once a minute. During deploys, gateways drain gradually and tell clients to reconnect with jittered delays so 100 k sockets do not reconnect in the same second.

deepDives.title: Multi-device sync and offline catch-up
deepDives.problem: Alice has a phone, a tablet and a laptop. Each is online at different times. Each must end up with every message, in order, plus the right unread counts, without asking every conversation 'anything new?' on every reconnect.

options.name: Per-conversation cursors
options.how: Each device remembers the last seq per conversation and asks each conversation on reconnect.
cons: A user in 400 conversations makes 400 queries every reconnect
Mostly empty answers

options.name: Per-user inbox with one cursor per device
options.how: For every message, append a pointer to each member's inbox with an increasing inboxSeq. A device syncs with one range read after its last inboxSeq.
pros: Reconnect is one query, sized by what was missed
Read-state and receipts can ride the same log
cons: Write amplification of one pointer per member
Large groups multiply that

deepDives.choice: Per-user inbox for groups up to 500. At 1.5 recipients on average this is about 350 k small pointer writes/s, or about 580 k/s counting the sender's own inbox (231 k × 2.5) so her other devices see what she sent. A Cassandra cluster handles that. Read-state changes from one device are written as events in the same inbox so other devices pick them up. A device that has been offline longer than the 30-day retention does a full resync of recent conversations. For broadcast channels with 100 k+ members I would not fan out pointers; those clients pull per channel, like the news-feed celebrity case.

failures: A gateway server dies with 100 k sockets
Clients reconnect with jittered backoff to other gateways and sync from their inbox cursor; registry entries for the dead gateway expire by TTL.
Pub/sub bus loses a live delivery event
No message lost: it is already in the inbox. The device notices a gap or gets it on next sync; a periodic light sync every few minutes covers silent losses.
MySQL shard holding conversation counters fails over
Promote the replica with semi-sync replication so no seq is reused; clients retry with the same clientMsgId and the dedupe check prevents duplicates.
Writes at quorum go to other replicas; reads at quorum; hinted handoff repairs later.
Mass reconnect after a regional network blip
Connection admission rate limits per gateway, randomized reconnect delays in clients, and sync served in pages.
Offline users still get messages on next app open; queue push notifications and retry with backoff.
scale: 10× traffic: more MySQL shards for counters (or move to the single-writer model), more Cassandra nodes, and 20 000 gateways; the architecture does not change.
Global users: gateways in many regions close to users; a conversation has a home region for ordering, and cross-region messages hop over a backbone, adding ~100 ms for international chats.
Huge broadcast channels: switch those to pull with a cached recent-message window, no per-member inbox writes and no per-member receipts.

followups.q: How do you make sure a retried message is not shown twice?
answer: The phone generates clientMsgId once and reuses it on retry.
The chat service keeps (conversationId, clientMsgId) to seq in a short-TTL cache plus a unique index, and returns the original seq on a duplicate.
The server stores and forwards ciphertext; ordering, receipts and routing still work since they use metadata.
Each device has its own keys, so the sender encrypts per device and the fan-out is per device, not per user.
Push previews and server-side history for brand-new devices are lost unless the user backs up keys.

followups.q: How does the typing indicator work at this scale?
answer: Ephemeral event over the socket, never stored.
Throttled on the client to one every 3 s and only sent to members who have that chat open.

followups.q: How do you deliver to a user with 4 devices on different gateways?
answer: The registry holds all four device sessions.
Publish once per gateway, carrying the device list for that gateway.
Each device acks independently and keeps its own cursor.

followups.q: How do you store unread counts?
answer: Unread for a conversation is lastSeq minus readUpTo; compute it, do not count rows.
The total badge is the sum over conversations, cached per user and updated on message and read events.

mistakes: Ordering messages by client or server timestamp and calling it done.
Writing every heartbeat to a database, or pushing every presence flap to every contact.
Keeping chat logic inside the WebSocket servers so every deploy drops millions of connections and state.
Storing a receipt row per message per member in large groups.
Assuming 'user online' means one device and forgetting multi-device sync.

Stored messages durably before acknowledging the sender
Delivered missed messages on reconnect and sent push notifications to offline users
Estimated messages per second and number of concurrent connections
senior: Ordered messages with a per-conversation sequence number and explained why timestamps fail
Used client message IDs for idempotent retries
Separated stateful gateways from stateless chat logic with a session registry for routing
Modeled receipts as delivered and read watermarks per member
Designed reconnect sync with a cursor per device
staff: Showed presence publishes only transitions, with grace periods and lazy subscription, using the heartbeat math
Explained the switch to a pull model for very large groups and channels
Covered deploy and mass-reconnect behaviour (draining, jitter, admission control)
Described what end-to-end encryption changes in fan-out, push and history
